rows.answer: Nike’s Greater China gross margin was **46.0% in fiscal 2025** (year ended May 31, 2025), down **420 basis points** from **50.2% in fiscal 2024**. [1]
NIKE Direct accounted for **46.4%** of Nike’s North America revenues in fiscal 2025, calculated as **$9,088 million ÷ $19,572 million**. [1]

Nike’s Europe, Middle East and Africa (EMEA) revenue fell **10% to $12.257 billion in fiscal 2025 from $13.607 billion in fiscal 2024**, and the decline was also **10% excluding currency changes**, so foreign exchange was not the primary cause. [1]

The decrease reflected lower demand across **Men’s, the Jordan Brand, Kids’ and Women’s**. By channel, wholesale revenue declined **6%**, while NIKE Direct revenue fell **16%**, driven by a **30% decline in digital sales** that was only partly offset by **5% growth in store sales**. [1] Product revenue also weakened: footwear declined **10%** and apparel **9%** on a currency-neutral basis, reflecting lower unit sales and lower average selling prices caused mainly by channel/product mix changes and higher discounts. [1]
Nike returned **$5.3 billion to shareholders in fiscal 2025** through share repurchases and dividends. Its inventories were **$7.5 billion as of May 31, 2025**, unchanged from the prior year. [1]
Lululemon’s sales per square foot **decreased by $35, from $1,609 in fiscal 2023 to $1,574 in fiscal 2024**—a **2.2% decline**. Fiscal 2024 ended February 2, 2025. [1]

Men’s products accounted for **24% of Lululemon’s 2024 net revenue**. The reported amounts were **$2.558 billion in men’s product revenue** out of **$10.588 billion total net revenue**, equivalent to **24.16%** before rounding. [1][2]

Lululemon’s inventory was **$1.442 billion** at the end of fiscal 2024 (**February 2, 2025**), comprising inventories at cost of $1.526 billion less provisions and reserves. [1]

It had increased **9%** from $1.324 billion at the end of fiscal 2023, and Lululemon expects inventory to continue growing in fiscal 2025, with the growth rate **exceeding net revenue growth**. [2][1]
Lululemon’s diluted earnings per share grew **20.0%** in fiscal 2024, from **$12.20 in 2023** to **$14.64 in 2024**. [1][2]

In Under Armour’s fiscal 2025, ended March 31, 2025:

- **Wholesale revenue** fell **8.1%**, from **$3.243 billion in fiscal 2024 to $2.979 billion**—a decrease of **$264.3 million**. [1]
- **Direct-to-consumer revenue** fell **10.5%**, from **$2.335 billion to $2.090 billion**—a decrease of **$245.5 million**. [1]

The declines reflected lower wholesale demand and reduced discounting and promotional activity in the direct-to-consumer channel, particularly e-commerce. [2]
Footwear accounted for **23.4%** of Under Armour’s fiscal 2025 total net revenues (**$1.206 billion ÷ $5.164 billion**). Under Armour’s fiscal year ended **March 31, 2025**. [1]
Under Armour paid **$434 million** to settle the consolidated securities class action. The payment was funded with **balance-sheet cash and $63 million of insurance proceeds**. [1]

Under Armour’s inventory balance was **$945.836 million as of March 31, 2025**, compared with **$958.495 million as of March 31, 2024**. It therefore **decreased by $12.659 million, or approximately 1.3%**, year over year. [1]

Columbia Sportswear’s gross margin expanded by **60 basis points, from 49.6% in 2023 to 50.2% in 2024** (fiscal year ended December 31, 2024). The main drivers were:

- **Favorable inbound freight costs**
- **Favorable regional and channel sales mix**

These benefits were partly offset by **lower channel profitability due to increased clearance and promotional activity**. [1]

Columbia Sportswear’s Profit Improvement Program delivered approximately **$90 million in realized cost savings in fiscal 2024**, net of approximately **$3 million–$4 million in severance and other costs**. [1]

Columbia Sportswear’s inventory decreased **7% in 2024**, falling to **$690.5 million at December 31, 2024**, from **$746.3 million a year earlier**. The decline reflected lower inventory purchases and the use of outlet stores and temporary clearance locations to sell excess merchandise. [1][2]

The company expects healthier inventories—both its own and those of wholesale partners—to support **gross-margin expansion in 2025**, partly by reducing the need for clearance activity and promotions. [1]
Columbia Sportswear’s SOREL brand net sales fell **29.2%** in 2024, from **$336.688 million in 2023 to $238.266 million in 2024**—reported as a **29% decrease**. [1]
In fiscal 2025, **Deckers’ operating margin was 23.6%**, and **diluted earnings per share were $6.33**. The fiscal year ended **March 31, 2025**. [1][2]

In fiscal 2025, ended March 31, 2025, Deckers’ **wholesale channel** grew **17.4%**, increasing from **$2,432,307 thousand** to **$2,855,865 thousand**—a **$423,558 thousand** increase. Its **direct-to-consumer (DTC) channel** grew **14.8%**, from **$1,855,456 thousand** to **$2,129,747 thousand**—up **$274,291 thousand**. Thus, wholesale grew faster than DTC in both percentage and absolute dollar terms. [1][2]
Deckers’ inventories increased by **4.4%**, from **$474.311 million on March 31, 2024** to **$495.226 million on March 31, 2025**. [1]
Deckers repurchased **765,321 shares** after fiscal 2025 ended (March 31, 2025) through **May 9, 2025**, at a **weighted-average price of $109.75 per share**. [1][2]
